title: Ranges in C++20
learningGoals: build a pipeline with the pipe symbol
sort a whole vector with ranges sort

youtube.title: C++20 Ranges and Views: filter, transform, take | C++ Programming EP 79
youtube.description: In this episode you will build a pipeline with the pipe symbol, filter and transform lazily and sort a whole vector with ranges sort, with Xecxec the crab. 0:00 Intro · 0:15 Ranges in C++20 · 1:09 Filter then transform · 2:18 The pipeline · 2:53 Second program · 4:02 Recap · 4:32 Bug of the Day · 5:20 Challenge · 5:42 Next episode

thumbnail.pose: Xecxec next to a conveyor belt with a filter gate and a squash press

scenes.animation: Tomato title card: EP sticker thuds in, title stamps with a whoosh, Xecxec scuttles in and waves; thud, whoosh, claw-click, sting
scenes.narration: Today we meet ranges, new in C plus plus twenty. They let you chain steps with the pipe symbol, like a conveyor belt.

scenes.onScreen: "Ranges in C++20": numbered lines (1. A view does not copy the data; 2. The pipe symbol joins stations; 3. Views work only when you read them) and an analogy card: a conveyor belt: each station changes the items that pass
scenes.animation: Lines spring in one by one with a pop; the analogy card slides in from the right
scenes.narration: A view is a lazy window on a range. It does not copy the data, and it does no work until you read it. You join views with the pipe symbol. Think of a conveyor belt. Each station changes the items that pass, one at a time. Ranges in C plus plus twenty make code read like a recipe. Take the numbers, keep the even ones, and square them. Views are lazy. They do no work until you ask for an item. They also copy nothing, so they use almost no memory.
points: A view does not copy the data
Views work only when you read them

analogy.title: Ranges in C++20
analogy.body: A conveyor belt: each station changes the items that pass

scenes.onScreen: ranges.cpp: even numbers are kept, then squared, then printed
scenes.animation: Code types in with key-tick; butter [HL n] highlight sweeps line by line with marker-swipe; explanation card on the right
scenes.narration: [HL 10] The pipe sends the vector into a filter station. The lambda keeps only even numbers. [HL 11] The next station squares each number that passes. [HL 12] Nothing runs until this loop reads the view. The output is four sixteen thirty-six sixty-four. [HL 16] Ranges sort takes the whole vector, and no iterators. Greater sorts from big to small. [HL 17] The first value is eight. [HL 10] The pipe sends the vector into a filter. The filter keeps only the even numbers. [HL 11] The next pipe sends the result into a transform, which squares each item. [HL 12] The loop asks for the items, and now the work happens. The output is four, sixteen, thirty-six, sixty-four. [HL 16] The ranges sort takes the whole vector, and the greater function sorts in the other direction.

scenes.onScreen: a flow from the vector, through the filter, to the transform
scenes.animation: Steps drop in left to right with a pop; connecting arrows draw on; the active step glows butter
scenes.narration: The data flows left to right. The vector goes into the filter. The filter keeps the even numbers. The transform squares them. The loop pulls the values out one by one. Notice the stations on the conveyor belt. Each item goes through all the stations before the next item starts. No station keeps a full copy of the data.

diagram.caption: a flow from the vector, through the filter, to the transform

scenes.onScreen: iota.cpp: an endless counter is cut to the first five numbers
scenes.animation: Second program or a twist on the first; [HL n] and [TRACK name=value] cues drive the variable tracker; output panel fills line by line with a ding per line
scenes.narration: [HL 6] Iota makes an endless counter that starts at one. It does not fill memory, because a view is lazy. [HL 6] Take cuts the counter after five items. The output is one two three four five. [HL 6] Iota makes numbers that start at one and never end. It is safe, because the numbers are made only when asked for. [HL 6] Take stops after five items. The loop prints one to five.

scenes.animation: Dark-blue terminal: the compile command types with key-tick, the run command types, output prints in mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Save the file as iota dot cpp. Compile it with g plus plus. Then run the program. The program prints the squares of the even numbers, then eight, then one to five. Notice that an endless range is fine here. The take view cuts it after five items.

scenes.animation: Recap lines tick in one by one with a pop; Xecxec nods after each tick
scenes.narration: Let us recap. One. A view is a lazy window on a range. Two. The pipe symbol joins stations. Three. Views copy no data. Four. Ranges sort takes the whole container. Pause the video. Say these ideas out loud, one time, slowly.
points: A view is a lazy window on a range.
Ranges sort takes the whole container.

scenes.onScreen: BUG OF THE DAY: A missing header
scenes.animation: Butter banner drops in with a buzzer; wrong code shakes; the g++ error lines appear in tomato; the fix slides in and the terminal turns mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Bug of the Day. We use views without the ranges header. The compiler says views has not been declared. Add the include line for ranges. Ranges need the right header and a modern compiler setting. If the compiler says that views is not a member of std, check two things. Is the ranges header there, and did you pass the flag for C plus plus twenty?

scenes.onScreen: Why did the view stay calm? It never copied anything, so it had nothing to lose.
scenes.animation: Full tomato screen, card flips in with a rimshot, Xecxec snaps his claw
scenes.narration: Why did the view stay calm? It never copied anything, so it had nothing to lose.

scenes.onScreen: Task card: keep the odd numbers
scenes.animation: Task card pops in; checklist ticks with a pop; Xecxec holds a tiny pen
scenes.narration: Your challenge: Use a filter view to print only the odd numbers of a vector. Hint: the filter lambda tests that the remainder after dividing by two equals one. Write your answer in the comments.

scenes.animation: Next-episode card slides up with a whoosh; right side stays empty for end-screen elements; sign-off text types in
scenes.narration: Next time: move semantics. Keep coding, says Xecxec!

bug.error:
Compiler output (exactly as g++ prints it):

rangebug.cpp: In function 'int main()':
rangebug.cpp:7:22: error: 'views' has not been declared
    7 |     for (int x : v | views::take(2)) {
      |                      ^~~~~
bug.why: Views live in the ranges header. Include it. Also compile with the C plus plus twenty flag.

pun: "Why did the view stay calm? It never copied anything, so it had nothing to lose."
challenge: Use a filter view to print only the odd numbers of a vector. Hint: the filter lambda tests that the remainder after dividing by two equals one.
challengeAnswer: Pipe the vector into views filter. The lambda returns x modulo two not equal to zero. Print the view with a loop.
